120	We should start simple, like comparing normal and async function calls and
121	later expand to other techniques.
122	
123	## Usage
124	
125	```
126	iiac-perf [BENCH...] [--runs N] [-d SECONDS] [-o OUTER] [-i INNER]
127	iiac-perf qualify-environment [--runs N] [--run-sleep SPAN] [-d SECONDS]
128	iiac-perf suggest-freq BENCH [-d SECONDS] [--pin-cpus CPUS]
129	```
130	
131	`BENCH` is one or more registered bench names, or `all` for every
132	registered bench. A name that matches no bench exactly runs every
133	bench it is a prefix of: `ice` runs all iceoryx2 benches, `mpsc`
134	runs `mpsc-1t` and `mpsc-2t`. A name that is no prefix either runs
135	every bench it matches as a regular expression: `zcr-[sm]psc-v[23]`
136	runs the v2 and v3 pairs of both rings. **With no arguments, `iiac-perf` prints the
137	available list and exits, and that's the source of truth for which
138	benches the current build registers.**
139	
140	The commands, every flag, and shell completion are in
141	[docs/usage.md](docs/usage.md). A quick taste:
142	
143	```
144	iiac-perf all                                 # every bench, ten runs of 0.25 s each
145	iiac-perf mpsc-2t --pin-cpus 0,1              # pinned to two CPUs, same CCX
146	iiac-perf zcr-spsc-v4 --pin-cpus all         # at every placement the host declares, then a table
147	iiac-perf min-now --blocks 10 --block-warmup 2ms   # ten replicates, post-wake ramp discarded
148	sudo iiac-perf suggest-freq zcr-mpsc-v0-2t --pin-cpus 0,12   # find the pin frequency
149	```
150	
151	Every run flag has a config key, so a box can set its
152	replication once and a run needs no flags: `blocks`,
153	`block_sleep`, `block_warmup`, and the rest in
154	[docs/config.md](docs/config.md), with
155	[iiac-perf.example.md](iiac-perf.example.md) as the starting
156	file, which `iiac-perf init-config PATH` writes. Every
157	run has a hundred blocks by default, so each carries an error bar
158	without a config at all.
159	
160	### Config files
161	
162	A config names the benches as well as the knobs, so a whole run
163	is a file: `iiac-perf queue.md`. Every run flag has a key, and the
164	report's `Config:` list shows every value with where it came from,
165	a file, a flag, or `(default)`, so what applied is never a guess.
166	The full reference is [docs/config.md](docs/config.md).
167	
168	#### Which files are read
169	
170	A plain run layers up to two files under the flags, and for any
171	key the nearest file that sets it wins:
172	
173	| Order | File | What it is for |
174	|---|---|---|
175	| 1 | built-in defaults | every key has one, or is off |
176	| 2 | `~/.config/iiac-perf/config.md` | the host: its `[freq]` clock steady state, its pin `[profiles]` |
177	| 3 | the nearest `iiac-perf.md`, this directory then each parent | a project's or a tree's defaults |
178	| 4 | flags on the line | this run |
179	
180	The search for `iiac-perf.md` stops at the first found, so a file
181	high in a tree is what the directories below fall back to, never a
182	layer under a nearer one. `[tags]` and `[profiles]` merge by entry,
183	and `[freq]` replaces whole.
184	
185	A named config changes rows 2 and 3. Under `iiac-perf queue.md`, or
186	`--config queue`, the run keys come from `queue.md` and the defaults
187	alone, flags still winning, so the same file is the same run on
188	every host. The host's files then give only `[freq]` and
189	`[profiles]`, which describe the host rather than the run. The name
190	is looked for in this directory, each parent, then
191	`~/.config/iiac-perf/`, so a tree of bench directories shares a
192	parent's config by name.
193	
194	`[freq]` is the host's: the governor, EPP, boost, and clamp that
195	`restore-freq` and every pin's exit return to. No flag sets it and
196	`init-config` leaves it empty. `iiac-perf setup --apply` writes it
197	from the live state, and the host's `[profiles]` from its topology.
198	A run's pin is the separate key `pin_freq`.
199	
200	#### The commands
201	
202	| To | Run |
203	|---|---|
204	| see every key, commented out at its default | `iiac-perf init-config \| less` |
205	| turn a line that worked into a file | `iiac-perf init-config quick.md --benches min-now --blocks 10 -d 0.5s` |
206	| run a file | `iiac-perf quick.md` |
207	| run it with one thing changed, once | `iiac-perf quick.md --blocks 20`, or `iiac-perf quick.md std-now` |
208	| change a key in the file | `iiac-perf update-config quick.md --blocks 20` |
209	| bring an old file up to date | `iiac-perf update-config old.md --backup` |
210	| start a new file from another's values | `iiac-perf init-config --from old.md new.md` |
211	| start from the bare template | `iiac-perf init-config --from /dev/null new.md` |
212	| rerun what a record measured, on any host | `iiac-perf init-config --from-record file.jsonl new.toml` |
213	
214	`init-config` writes the run its line would make on this host: the
215	line's flags, over the run keys the host's files set, and it names
216	what it took from each file. It never writes over a file unless
217	`--backup` (keeps `PATH.bak`) or `--overwrite` (keeps nothing) says
218	so, and the old file's values are then gone. `update-config` keeps
219	them: it sets the line's flags over the file's own values and
220	rewrites it in place, checked before it is touched, `--backup`
221	keeping the old file. Either rewrite loses prose the author added.
222	
223	#### The two carriers
224	
225	A `.md` config is a document whose `toml` fences, read in order,
226	are the config, so the prose between them explains each key. A
227	`.toml` config is the keys under ruled section headings, with no
228	prose, since as comments the prose buries the keys. In both, a
229	commented-out key has no space after its `#` and a comment has one:
230	
231	```toml
232	# ---- Blocks ----
233	
234	blocks = 10
235	#block_sleep = "1-10ms"
236	#block_warmup = "0"
237	```
238	
239	Top-level keys go before any table, in either carrier: a bare key
240	after `[tags]` would land inside it.
241	
242	#### From a line to a file, on two hosts
243	
244	```
245	iiac-perf --benches zcr-spsc-v3-2t -d 0.25s --blocks 10 --pin-freq      # a line that works
246	iiac-perf init-config configs/spsc.md --benches zcr-spsc-v3-2t -d 0.25s --blocks 10 --pin-freq
247	iiac-perf configs/spsc.md                                                # the same run
248	```
249	
250	Commit `configs/spsc.md`, pull it on the other host, and run the
251	same last line there. The two `Config:` lists then agree key for
252	key, each naming `configs/spsc.md` as the source, and differ only in
253	what is the host's: the `freq` row, and the clock the `pin_freq`
254	word resolves to there. To try a change once, add the flag,
255	and the list shows that flag as its key's source. To keep it,
256	`iiac-perf update-config configs/spsc.md --blocks 20`.
257	
258	#### When it stops
259	
260	| Message | Cause |
261	|---|---|
262	| ``unknown field `bogus`, expected one of ...`` | a key this version does not know: a typo, or a file from another version |
263	| `duration and total_duration are both set: keep one` | they are one choice, and one file made it twice |
264	| `a tag needs a record target, from --record-dir, --record-file, ...` | `[tags]` or `--tag` with nowhere to write them |
265	| `record: a path's shape no longer picks the mode, so the key is gone` | a file from before `record_dir` and `record_file` |
266	| `the run's config nope.md not found, in:` and the places tried | a named config that is in none of them |
267	| `queue.md exists, and is left as it is: --backup ... --overwrite ...` | `init-config` over a file, without saying so |
268	| `The [freq] in use is from iiac-perf.md.` ending a refusal | which file's `[freq]` a pin or restore refused |
269	| `warning: the [freq] from x.md is not the state this host runs at` | a table from another host: the restore will move this one to it |
270	
271	A malformed file is always an error, never a silent fallback to the
272	defaults.
273	
274	What a run prints, and what to conclude from it, is
275	[docs/report-guide.md](docs/report-guide.md).
276	
277	### Comparing
278	
279	One invocation's `LSC trimmed` says what that invocation could
280	resolve, not whether the claim holds across invocations, and a
281	comparison is a question about two sets of invocations. So record
282	the runs, repeat them, and let `analyze` read them back:
283	
284	```
285	# the benches to compare, in one invocation, repeated five times into one file
286	for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
287	  iiac-perf zcr-mpsc-v2-2t zcr-mpsc-v2-2t-nop zcr-mpsc-v2-2t-store-seqcst \
288	    --record-file runs/control.jsonl
289	done
290	
291	# each bench's invocations against themselves: spread, claim, calibration
292	iiac-perf analyze runs/control.jsonl
293	
294	# the ladder: each bench against the first, and against the one before
295	iiac-perf analyze runs/control.jsonl --compare
296	```
297	
298	A bare `--compare` compares every bench the records hold, in the
299	order each first ran. `--compare KEY` does the same for any key, a
300	tag or `bench`, `host`, `placement`, `binary`, or `file`, and `--compare KEY=A,B,...` names
301	the sides and their order, two or more of them. Two are one
302	comparison, B against A. Three or more are a ladder: each side
303	against the first and against the one before, so `A,B,C` prints
304	A -> B, A -> C, and B -> C. `--compare` repeats, each adding its
305	pairs, so for A -> B and A -> C alone:
306	
307	```
308	iiac-perf analyze runs/control.jsonl \
309	  --compare bench=zcr-mpsc-v2-2t,zcr-mpsc-v2-2t-nop \
310	  --compare bench=zcr-mpsc-v2-2t,zcr-mpsc-v2-2t-store-seqcst
311	```
312	
313	By what is compared:
314	
315	| to compare | run | then |
316	|---|---|---|
317	| two benches, or versions of one | them in one invocation, repeated | `--compare bench=A,B` |
318	| two conditions | each tagged, `--tag cond=A` and `--tag cond=B`, alternating | `--compare cond=A,B` |
319	| two sessions | each into its own file | `analyze a.jsonl b.jsonl --compare file=a.jsonl,b.jsonl` |
320	
321	Each row says `detected`, or `not seen, below N%`, what it could
322	have seen. Benches in one invocation pair by it, and sides that
323	alternate in time pair as neighbours, so a drift between
324	invocations cancels. One invocation a side pairs as `one each`,
325	the weakest claim, so repeat. The notes name any run parameter the
326	two sides ran differently, and warn when they ran hours apart or
327	when more than one binary measured them.
328	
329	To see what a claim summarizes, draw the runs: `iiac-perf figures
330	runs/control.jsonl --show trim --out control.png` puts each run's
331	block means in a panel per bench and invocation, the runs the trim
332	drops in grey.
333	
334	Two builds of the same code can read several percent apart, since
335	where the code lands in memory moves a bench's level: adding one
336	function moved `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` by 3.7% on the 3900X. So a variant
337	of a bench is compared against a `-nop` twin, the same change
338	doing nothing, and not only against the original. `analyze` is in
339	[docs/usage.md](docs/usage.md), and the statistics in
340	[docs/statistics.md](docs/statistics.md).
341	
342	## Testing
343	
344	```
345	cargo test                                    # normal run
346	cargo test -- --nocapture                     # show eprintln diagnostics
347	taskset -c 0 cargo test -- --nocapture        # restrict to 1 CPU
348	```
349

is a file: `iiac-perf queue.md`. Every run flag has a key, and the
report's `Config:` list shows every value with where it came from,
a file, a flag, or `(default)`, so what applied is never a guess.
The full reference is [docs/config.md](docs/config.md).

#### Which files are read

A plain run layers up to two files under the flags, and for any
key the nearest file that sets it wins:

| Order | File | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | built-in defaults | every key has one, or is off |
| 2 | `~/.config/iiac-perf/config.md` | the host: its `[freq]` clock steady state, its pin `[profiles]` |
| 3 | the nearest `iiac-perf.md`, this directory then each parent | a project's or a tree's defaults |
| 4 | flags on the line | this run |

The search for `iiac-perf.md` stops at the first found, so a file
high in a tree is what the directories below fall back to, never a
layer under a nearer one. `[tags]` and `[profiles]` merge by entry,
and `[freq]` replaces whole.

A named config changes rows 2 and 3. Under `iiac-perf queue.md`, or
`--config queue`, the run keys come from `queue.md` and the defaults
alone, flags still winning, so the same file is the same run on
every host. The host's files then give only `[freq]` and
`[profiles]`, which describe the host rather than the run. The name
is looked for in this directory, each parent, then
`~/.config/iiac-perf/`, so a tree of bench directories shares a
parent's config by name.

`[freq]` is the host's: the governor, EPP, boost, and clamp that
`restore-freq` and every pin's exit return to. No flag sets it and
`init-config` leaves it empty. `iiac-perf setup --apply` writes it
from the live state, and the host's `[profiles]` from its topology.
A run's pin is the separate key `pin_freq`.

#### The commands

| To | Run |
|---|---|
| see every key, commented out at its default | `iiac-perf init-config \| less` |
| turn a line that worked into a file | `iiac-perf init-config quick.md --benches min-now --blocks 10 -d 0.5s` |
| run a file | `iiac-perf quick.md` |
| run it with one thing changed, once | `iiac-perf quick.md --blocks 20`, or `iiac-perf quick.md std-now` |
| change a key in the file | `iiac-perf update-config quick.md --blocks 20` |
| bring an old file up to date | `iiac-perf update-config old.md --backup` |
| start a new file from another's values | `iiac-perf init-config --from old.md new.md` |
| start from the bare template | `iiac-perf init-config --from /dev/null new.md` |
| rerun what a record measured, on any host | `iiac-perf init-config --from-record file.jsonl new.toml` |

`init-config` writes the run its line would make on this host: the
line's flags, over the run keys the host's files set, and it names
what it took from each file. It never writes over a file unless
`--backup` (keeps `PATH.bak`) or `--overwrite` (keeps nothing) says
so, and the old file's values are then gone. `update-config` keeps
them: it sets the line's flags over the file's own values and
rewrites it in place, checked before it is touched, `--backup`
keeping the old file. Either rewrite loses prose the author added.

#### The two carriers

A `.md` config is a document whose `toml` fences, read in order,
are the config, so the prose between them explains each key. A
`.toml` config is the keys under ruled section headings, with no
prose, since as comments the prose buries the keys. In both, a
commented-out key has no space after its `#` and a comment has one:

```toml
# ---- Blocks ----

blocks = 10
#block_sleep = "1-10ms"
#block_warmup = "0"
```

Top-level keys go before any table, in either carrier: a bare key
after `[tags]` would land inside it.

#### From a line to a file, on two hosts

```
iiac-perf --benches zcr-spsc-v3-2t -d 0.25s --blocks 10 --pin-freq      # a line that works
iiac-perf init-config configs/spsc.md --benches zcr-spsc-v3-2t -d 0.25s --blocks 10 --pin-freq
iiac-perf configs/spsc.md                                                # the same run
```

Commit `configs/spsc.md`, pull it on the other host, and run the
same last line there. The two `Config:` lists then agree key for
key, each naming `configs/spsc.md` as the source, and differ only in
what is the host's: the `freq` row, and the clock the `pin_freq`
word resolves to there. To try a change once, add the flag,
and the list shows that flag as its key's source. To keep it,
`iiac-perf update-config configs/spsc.md --blocks 20`.

#### When it stops

| Message | Cause |
|---|---|
| ``unknown field `bogus`, expected one of ...`` | a key this version does not know: a typo, or a file from another version |
| `duration and total_duration are both set: keep one` | they are one choice, and one file made it twice |
| `a tag needs a record target, from --record-dir, --record-file, ...` | `[tags]` or `--tag` with nowhere to write them |
| `record: a path's shape no longer picks the mode, so the key is gone` | a file from before `record_dir` and `record_file` |
| `the run's config nope.md not found, in:` and the places tried | a named config that is in none of them |
| `queue.md exists, and is left as it is: --backup ... --overwrite ...` | `init-config` over a file, without saying so |
| `The [freq] in use is from iiac-perf.md.` ending a refusal | which file's `[freq]` a pin or restore refused |
| `warning: the [freq] from x.md is not the state this host runs at` | a table from another host: the restore will move this one to it |

A malformed file is always an error, never a silent fallback to the
defaults.

What a run prints, and what to conclude from it, is
[docs/report-guide.md](docs/report-guide.md).

### Comparing

One invocation's `LSC trimmed` says what that invocation could
resolve, not whether the claim holds across invocations, and a
comparison is a question about two sets of invocations. So record
the runs, repeat them, and let `analyze` read them back:

```
# the benches to compare, in one invocation, repeated five times into one file
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  iiac-perf zcr-mpsc-v2-2t zcr-mpsc-v2-2t-nop zcr-mpsc-v2-2t-store-seqcst \
    --record-file runs/control.jsonl
done

# each bench's invocations against themselves: spread, claim, calibration
iiac-perf analyze runs/control.jsonl

# the ladder: each bench against the first, and against the one before
iiac-perf analyze runs/control.jsonl --compare
```

A bare `--compare` compares every bench the records hold, in the
order each first ran. `--compare KEY` does the same for any key, a
tag or `bench`, `host`, `placement`, `binary`, or `file`, and `--compare KEY=A,B,...` names
the sides and their order, two or more of them. Two are one
comparison, B against A. Three or more are a ladder: each side
against the first and against the one before, so `A,B,C` prints
A -> B, A -> C, and B -> C. `--compare` repeats, each adding its
pairs, so for A -> B and A -> C alone:

```
iiac-perf analyze runs/control.jsonl \
  --compare bench=zcr-mpsc-v2-2t,zcr-mpsc-v2-2t-nop \
  --compare bench=zcr-mpsc-v2-2t,zcr-mpsc-v2-2t-store-seqcst
```

By what is compared:

| to compare | run | then |
|---|---|---|
| two benches, or versions of one | them in one invocation, repeated | `--compare bench=A,B` |
| two conditions | each tagged, `--tag cond=A` and `--tag cond=B`, alternating | `--compare cond=A,B` |
| two sessions | each into its own file | `analyze a.jsonl b.jsonl --compare file=a.jsonl,b.jsonl` |

Each row says `detected`, or `not seen, below N%`, what it could
have seen. Benches in one invocation pair by it, and sides that
alternate in time pair as neighbours, so a drift between
invocations cancels. One invocation a side pairs as `one each`,
the weakest claim, so repeat. The notes name any run parameter the
two sides ran differently, and warn when they ran hours apart or
when more than one binary measured them.

To see what a claim summarizes, draw the runs: `iiac-perf figures
runs/control.jsonl --show trim --out control.png` puts each run's
block means in a panel per bench and invocation, the runs the trim
drops in grey.

Two builds of the same code can read several percent apart, since
where the code lands in memory moves a bench's level: adding one
function moved `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` by 3.7% on the 3900X. So a variant
of a bench is compared against a `-nop` twin, the same change
doing nothing, and not only against the original. `analyze` is in
[docs/usage.md](docs/usage.md), and the statistics in
[docs/statistics.md](docs/statistics.md).

## Testing

```
cargo test                                    # normal run
cargo test -- --nocapture                     # show eprintln diagnostics
taskset -c 0 cargo test -- --nocapture        # restrict to 1 CPU
```

the three the bare command prints the bench list. None by default, so a benchmark directory's
`iiac-perf.md` is its natural home.

#benches = ["zcr-mpsc-v0-2t", "zcr-mpsc-v1-2t"]
```

`duration` is the target wall-clock seconds per bench, the `-d` default. `-d` on the line overrides
it, and so does `-D`, a total budget split across every run of every bench.

choice, so a file sets one of them, and the nearer file's choice clears the other.

side by side, which teaches the vocabulary.

content.text:
The dev build is installed as `iiac-perf-dev`, so from the repo directory:

```
# both new benches, prefix match
iiac-perf-dev zcr-mpsc-v3 --pin-freq=no

# one of them
iiac-perf-dev zcr-mpsc-v3-2t --pin-freq=no

# one quick run each instead of ten
iiac-perf-dev zcr-mpsc-v3 --runs 1 --pin-freq=no
```

`--pin-freq=no` is only needed on this laptop, where the default clock pin fails; on the 3900X or 7600X leave it off.

To compare against v2, record five invocations into one file and let `analyze` read them back:

```
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  iiac-perf-dev zcr-mpsc-v2-1t zcr-mpsc-v3-1t zcr-mpsc-v2-2t zcr-mpsc-v3-2t \
    --pin-freq=no --record-file tmp/mpsc-v3.jsonl
done

iiac-perf-dev analyze tmp/mpsc-v3.jsonl \
  --compare bench=zcr-mpsc-v2-1t,zcr-mpsc-v3-1t \
  --compare bench=zcr-mpsc-v2-2t,zcr-mpsc-v3-2t
```

I have run the `--runs 1` form here; the loop and the `analyze` step I have not, and they follow the README's "Comparing" section. At ten runs per bench each invocation takes several minutes.

Add `--pin-cpus all` to an invocation to run every placement the host declares (here `smt`, `ccx` and unpinned) and end with a table of benches by placement.

content.text:
Give the clock as a number, since this host has no `pin_mhz` for the bare flag to resolve:

```
iiac-perf-dev zcr-mpsc-v3 --pin-freq=2400 --pin-cpus smt
```

I ran `zcr-mpsc-v3-2t` that way once just now and it works: the clock pinned at 2400 MHz with boost off, the threads on CPUs 3 and 7 (the `smt` pair), and the host's `[freq]` restored on exit. That run read about 109 ns per round trip with every switch count zero.

2400 MHz is the i5-1135G7's base frequency, and `smt` is already the default placement here, so `--pin-cpus smt` only makes it explicit.

For the comparison with v2, the same two flags replace `--pin-freq=no`:

```
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  iiac-perf-dev zcr-mpsc-v2-1t zcr-mpsc-v3-1t zcr-mpsc-v2-2t zcr-mpsc-v3-2t \
    --pin-freq=2400 --pin-cpus smt --record-file tmp/mpsc-v3.jsonl
done

iiac-perf-dev analyze tmp/mpsc-v3.jsonl \
  --compare bench=zcr-mpsc-v2-1t,zcr-mpsc-v3-1t \
  --compare bench=zcr-mpsc-v2-2t,zcr-mpsc-v3-2t
```

To make the bare `--pin-freq` and the default run work here, add `pin_mhz = 2400` under `[freq]` in `~/.config/iiac-perf/config.md`. I have not changed that file.

The single and one-segment pairs are in the working copy, and validation passes.

**What changed**
- **Four benches**: `zcr-mpsc-v3-1t-1seg`, `-2t-1seg`, `-1t-single` and `-2t-single`, as registry entries over the generic bench.
- **Registry test**: it now treats `-1t-` inside a name as one thread, so the variant stays after the thread count.
- **No new unwrap sites**: the new entries reuse the existing ones.

**The comparison on this laptop** (five invocations, pinned at 2400 MHz on the `smt` pair, all 300 runs with zero switches):

| A -> B | A (ns) | B (ns) | difference | claim | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `1t-1seg` -> `1t-single` | 22.44 | 20.51 | -8.62% | 0.04% | detected |
| `2t-1seg` -> `2t-single` | 111.85 | 114.73 | +2.57% | 0.80% | detected |
| `1t` -> `1t-1seg` | 22.44 | 22.44 | 0.00% | 0.06% | not seen |
| `2t` -> `2t-1seg` | 111.91 | 111.85 | -0.05% | 0.65% | not seen |

- **`Multi` over one segment against two**: no difference seen, so the second segment costs nothing measurable when no switch happens.
- **`Single` against `Multi`**: faster on one thread, slower on two. I would not attribute either to the mode yet. `notes/build.md` records that code layout alone moved single benches up to 8% with this build's settings, and both differences are inside that. Whether the signs repeat on the measuring hosts and across placements is what will tell.

The plain version: with one thread, `Single` looks about 9% quicker than `Multi`; with two threads it looks slightly slower. Both gaps are small enough that they could come from where the compiler happened to place the code, so this needs repeating on the other machines before it means anything.

please review

The rung is flipped to `(done)` and fast validation passed after the edit.

**Title**

```
feat: the mpsc v3 single and one-segment pairs
```

**Body**

```
An mpsc v3 ring's segment mode is a type parameter, `Single` for one
segment with no switch compiled in and `Multi` for a ring that can
switch, and the bench pair runs `Multi` over two segments alone. So
nothing says whether `Single` buys anything, since it cannot have two
segments and the pair cannot be set beside it.

* The two modes are never measured over the same geometry.
  - The `-1seg` benches are `Multi` over one segment and the
    `-single` benches are `Single`, each at one thread and two, so
    the two differ in the mode alone.
  - The `-1seg` benches against the pair say what `Multi`'s second
    segment costs when no switch happens.
* A registry test took a name ending in `-1t` as one thread and any
  other as two, which a one-thread name with a variant after its
  thread count fails.
  - The test also takes `-1t-` inside a name, so a variant follows
    the thread count as the v2 variants' names have it.
```

content.text:
The futex pairs are in the working copy and full validation passes. All twelve mpsc v3 benches now exist.

**What changed**
- **Six benches**: a `-futex` twin of each of the six, as registry entries over the generic bench, using `Futex` at its default 10 ms timeout. Nobody ever sleeps, so the timeout never runs.
- **No new unwrap sites.**

**Futex against NoWake on this laptop** (five invocations of the twelve, pinned at 2400 MHz on the `smt` pair, all 600 runs with zero switches):

| bench | `NoWake` (ns) | `Futex` (ns) | difference | claim |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `1t` | 22.46 | 23.31 | +3.82% | 0.07% |
| `1t-1seg` | 22.45 | 23.32 | +3.86% | 0.05% |
| `1t-single` | 20.50 | 21.11 | +2.98% | 0.07% |
| `2t` | 114.33 | 117.98 | +3.19% | 0.50% |
| `2t-1seg` | 114.21 | 118.22 | +3.50% | 0.21% |
| `2t-single` | 115.16 | 116.31 | +0.99% | 0.38% |

- **Futex**: all six are detected and all six say `Futex` is slower, by 0.6 to 0.9 ns on one thread and 1.1 to 4.0 ns on two. The same sign in six different builds is more than code layout is likely to produce, so I think a ring that can sleep costs about 3 to 4% of a round trip here even when nobody sleeps.
- **`Single` on one thread**: faster under both wakes, -8.67% and -9.45%, which with the earlier -8.62% makes three agreeing readings. I think that gain is real.
- **`Single` on two threads**: the sign does not hold (+0.83% under `NoWake`, -1.62% under `Futex`, +2.57% in the earlier session), so no difference between the modes is shown there.
- **Caveat on two threads**: `zcr-mpsc-v3-2t` itself read 111.9 ns last session and 114.3 ns this one, from binaries one rung apart. That shift is the same size as the two-thread differences being read.

The plain version: making the ring able to sleep costs a little, about a nanosecond on one thread, every time, even if nothing ever sleeps. The one-segment-only mode is clearly quicker when one thread does both ends, and makes no visible difference when two threads hand off. These are laptop numbers; the measuring hosts still need to confirm them.

please review

The rung is flipped to `(done)` and fast validation passed after the edit.

**Title**

```
feat: the mpsc v3 futex pairs
```

**Body**

```
An mpsc v3 ring's wake is a type parameter: over `NoWake` a wait
polls and every wake check compiles out, and over `Futex` a full
producer or an empty consumer can sleep and be woken. The six
benches so far run `NoWake` alone, so nothing says what a ring that
can sleep pays on the message path when nobody sleeps.

* No bench runs a ring over a wake that sleeps.
  - A `-futex` twin of each of the six benches is the same ring, in
    the same mode over the same segments, over `Futex`.
  - Every wait still spins, so nobody sleeps, and a bench against
    its twin differs by the wake checks alone: the least a futex
    costs, not the cost of a sleep and a wake.
* The mode and the wake were not measured together.
  - With the twins the benches are every combination of the three
    segment shapes and the two wakes, at one thread and two.
```

May I commit and push this?

message.content: yes, commit and push

# How the build moves a bench

A bench's level belongs to the binary that measured it, not to its source alone. This file holds
what showed it, from `feat: spsc v4 benches` (2026-09-30 and 10-01), and the rules the repo took
from it. The guide's [Results by placement](../docs/report-guide.md#results-by-placement) and the
README's Building section are the user-facing side.

## What moved `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t`

Trimmed means at `smt`, ten runs an invocation, builds alternated in rounds and compared with
`analyze --compare build`. The noise floor, one binary in two sweeps an hour apart, is a median
0.06% (3900X) and 0.08% (7600X).

| change | 3900X | 7600X |
|---|---|---|
| rebuild of the same inputs | 0, byte-identical | 0 |
| version string only | +0.79%, not seen | +1.49% |
| an edit off the hot path, 16 codegen units | +7.61% | +1.08% |
| the same edit, one codegen unit | +0.25% | -0.90% |
| the same edit, fat LTO | +4.69% | -0.47% |
| the same edit, one codegen unit and forced alignment | +0.97% | -1.57% |
| rustc 1.98.1 against 1.98.0, same source | - | +2.04% |

- Under 16 codegen units an edit anywhere can move a hot function into another unit, where
  nothing inlines across: the `analyze` fix, which touched no bench, took the bench's `step` out of
  `run_adaptive` (10,819 bytes became 729 and 9,230), and the round trip rose 7.6%.
- One codegen unit and fat LTO give two trees one code shape, so what remains is where the hot loop
  falls against a cache line. LTO's pair differed only in `step`'s alignment (mod 64: 16 against
  0) and read 4.7% apart.
- Across every bench, the old tree against the new, the median change was 1.47% (3900X) and 0.82%
  (7600X) at the defaults then, 0.65% and 0.56% with one codegen unit, and 0.39% and 0.13% with
  forced alignment, which cost nothing overall (a median +0.04%) though single benches moved up to
  8%. Zen 2 is the more sensitive host.
- One unchanged binary drifts 1 to 2% between sessions days apart (the 7600X's 44.89, 45.04, and
  45.88 ns), where it repeats to 0.1% within an hour.
- The same commit, rustc, and flags built different binaries on the two x86 hosts at `b6b6404`,
  `924e69da617b5928` and `48512fa4f131f48e`: the 3900X's carries std source paths under
  `~/.rustup/toolchains/stable-…/lib/rustlib/src`, which we think its `rust-src` component puts
  there. Earlier both used an auto-installed toolchain without it and matched.

cat > notes/mpsc-v3-mode-wake.md <<'EOF'
# What mpsc v3's mode and wake cost

zc-ring-x1's `mpsc::v3` ring takes two type parameters, a segment mode, `Single` or `Multi`, and a
wake, `NoWake` or `Futex`. This file holds what the twelve `zcr-mpsc-v3` benches measured of them,
from `feat: mpsc v3 benches` (2026-10-04), and what that says about keeping the two parameters.

It rests on one session on one host, a laptop, and is provisional until the measuring hosts repeat
it ([Measure mpsc v3's mode and wake on the measuring
hosts](../TODO.md#measure-mpsc-v3s-mode-and-wake-on-the-measuring-hosts)).

## The session

- Host: an i5-1135G7 laptop, four cores and eight threads, `intel_pstate`, the clock pinned at
  2400 MHz, its base.
- Benches: `zcr-mpsc-v2-1t` and `-2t`, and the twelve `zcr-mpsc-v3` benches, against zc-ring-x1
  `83ab431`. Each v3 bench is v2's round trip with one message in flight, and every wait spins.
- Run: five invocations of the fourteen, ten runs each, at every placement the host declares:
  `smt`, CPUs 3 and 7, `ccx`, CPUs 3 and 2, two cores on the one L3, and unpinned. A one-thread
  bench has no `ccx` of its own.
- One binary, `e348cbb74d9f7c64`, built with rustc 1.99.0 from the tree one edit past `f27228d`,
  the version-of-record and `TODO.md` alone differing.
- Records: [records/mpsc-v3-fwlaptop.jsonl](../records/mpsc-v3-fwlaptop.jsonl), 1750 runs, every
  segment-switch count in them zero.
- Numbers are `analyze --compare`'s: each side's trimmed mean in ns, the difference as a percent
  of the first side's, and the claim, the smallest difference the pairing could call real.

## v3 against v2

`zcr-mpsc-v2` against `zcr-mpsc-v3`, `Multi` over two segments with `NoWake`, v2's geometry.

| bench | placement | v2 | v3 | d% | claim% | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `1t` | smt | 22.41 | 22.48 | +0.32 | 0.11 | detected |
| `1t` | unpinned | 22.40 | 22.48 | +0.36 | 0.08 | detected |
| `2t` | smt | 117.85 | 112.30 | -4.71 | 0.49 | detected |
| `2t` | ccx | 478.10 | 465.00 | -2.74 | 1.17 | detected |
| `2t` | unpinned | 486.91 | 471.71 | -3.12 | 2.42 | detected |

- At one thread v3 is 0.07 ns slower, a third of a percent.
- At two threads v3 is faster at every placement, by 3 to 5%.

## Multi over one segment against two

`zcr-mpsc-v3` against `zcr-mpsc-v3-*-1seg`, both `Multi` with `NoWake`.

| bench | placement | two | one | d% | claim% | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `1t` | smt | 22.48 | 22.47 | -0.02 | 0.06 | not seen |
| `1t` | unpinned | 22.48 | 22.48 | 0.00 | 0.03 | not seen |
| `2t` | smt | 112.30 | 112.31 | +0.01 | 0.40 | not seen |
| `2t` | ccx | 465.00 | 463.69 | -0.28 | 1.39 | not seen |
| `2t` | unpinned | 471.71 | 467.87 | -0.81 | 1.16 | not seen |

- A second segment costs nothing seen while no switch happens.

## Single against Multi over one segment

`-1seg` against `-single`, the geometry equal and the mode alone differing, under each wake.

| bench | wake | placement | `Multi` | `Single` | d% | claim% | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `1t` | `NoWake` | smt | 22.47 | 20.49 | -8.81 | 0.06 | detected |
| `1t` | `NoWake` | unpinned | 22.48 | 20.50 | -8.83 | 0.05 | detected |
| `1t` | `Futex` | smt | 23.31 | 21.11 | -9.45 | 0.06 | detected |
| `1t` | `Futex` | unpinned | 23.31 | 21.11 | -9.45 | 0.05 | detected |
| `2t` | `NoWake` | smt | 112.31 | 114.14 | +1.64 | 0.20 | detected |
| `2t` | `NoWake` | ccx | 463.69 | 459.80 | -0.84 | 1.00 | not seen |
| `2t` | `NoWake` | unpinned | 467.87 | 462.11 | -1.23 | 1.84 | not seen |
| `2t` | `Futex` | smt | 118.30 | 115.66 | -2.23 | 0.94 | detected |
| `2t` | `Futex` | ccx | 474.02 | 472.26 | -0.37 | 0.99 | not seen |
| `2t` | `Futex` | unpinned | 479.69 | 478.66 | -0.22 | 1.11 | not seen |

- At one thread `Single` is 2.0 to 2.2 ns faster, 9%, under both wakes and at both placements,
  and two earlier sessions of earlier binaries read the same, -8.62% and -8.67%.
- At two threads no difference holds: `not seen` four times of six, and the two `detected` at
  `smt` have opposite signs.

## Futex against NoWake

Each `NoWake` bench against its `-futex` twin. Nobody sleeps, so the difference is the wake checks
left on the message path, the producer's look at the waiting flag after its commit and the
consumer's fence at each half segment of releases, and not the cost of a sleep and a wake.

| bench | placement | `NoWake` | `Futex` | d% | claim% | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `1t` | smt | 22.48 | 23.31 | +3.69 | 0.09 | detected |
| `1t` | unpinned | 22.48 | 23.31 | +3.70 | 0.06 | detected |
| `1t-1seg` | smt | 22.47 | 23.31 | +3.72 | 0.08 | detected |
| `1t-1seg` | unpinned | 22.48 | 23.31 | +3.70 | 0.08 | detected |
| `1t-single` | smt | 20.49 | 21.11 | +2.99 | 0.03 | detected |
| `1t-single` | unpinned | 20.50 | 21.11 | +3.00 | 0.03 | detected |
| `2t` | smt | 112.30 | 118.66 | +5.67 | 0.32 | detected |
| `2t` | ccx | 465.00 | 478.97 | +3.00 | 0.96 | detected |
| `2t` | unpinned | 471.71 | 485.27 | +2.87 | 1.43 | detected |
| `2t-1seg` | smt | 112.31 | 118.30 | +5.34 | 0.80 | detected |
| `2t-1seg` | ccx | 463.69 | 474.02 | +2.23 | 1.00 | detected |
| `2t-1seg` | unpinned | 467.87 | 479.69 | +2.53 | 1.51 | detected |
| `2t-single` | smt | 114.14 | 115.66 | +1.33 | 0.84 | detected |
| `2t-single` | ccx | 459.80 | 472.26 | +2.71 | 0.90 | detected |
| `2t-single` | unpinned | 462.11 | 478.66 | +3.58 | 2.23 | detected |

- `Futex` is the slower in all fifteen: 0.6 to 0.8 ns at one thread, 3 to 4%, and 1.5 to 6.4 ns
  at `smt`, 10 to 14 ns at `ccx`, and 12 to 17 ns unpinned at two threads, 1 to 6%.

## What the numbers can carry

- One build of each bench: a mode or a wake is different code at different addresses, and with
  this repo's build settings layout alone moved single benches up to 8% ([build.md](build.md)).
  A difference in one bench at one placement is therefore not yet the parameter's.
- What repeats is: the `Futex` cost has one sign across fifteen rows of six benches, and the
  one-thread `Single` gain has one size across four rows and three sessions' binaries. We think
  both are the parameters' and not layout's.
- One host, and a laptop: its claims at two threads are 0.2 to 2.4%, where a measuring host's
  are tighter, and a ring's ranking has differed between hosts before
  ([Results by placement](../docs/report-guide.md#results-by-placement)).

## Whether the mode and the wake earn their place

Provisional, on the above, and zc-ring-x1's to decide.

- The mode: `Single` buys 2 ns of a 22 ns same-thread round trip and nothing shown where two
  threads hand off, which is what a ring between threads does, and `Multi` over one segment reads
  as `Multi` over two. We think the mode does not earn its place, and a ring that is always
  `Multi` loses only the same-thread case.
- The wake: a ring that can sleep pays 3 to 4% of every round trip when nobody sleeps, at every
  placement. We think that is too much to charge a ring that only spins, so the wake earns its
  place as a parameter unless its checks get cheaper, and what a sleep and a wake cost against a
  spin is not measured here.
EOF

# What mpsc v3's mode and wake cost

zc-ring-x1's `mpsc::v3` ring takes two type parameters, a segment mode, `Single` or `Multi`, and a
wake, `NoWake` or `Futex`. This file holds what the twelve `zcr-mpsc-v3` benches measured of them,
from `feat: mpsc v3 benches` (2026-10-04), and what that says about keeping the two parameters.

It rests on one session on one host, a laptop, and is provisional until the measuring hosts repeat
it ([Measure mpsc v3's mode and wake on the measuring
hosts](../TODO.md#measure-mpsc-v3s-mode-and-wake-on-the-measuring-hosts)).

## The session

- Host: an i5-1135G7 laptop, four cores and eight threads, `intel_pstate`, the clock pinned at
  2400 MHz, its base.
- Benches: `zcr-mpsc-v2-1t` and `-2t`, and the twelve `zcr-mpsc-v3` benches, against zc-ring-x1
  `83ab431`. Each v3 bench is v2's round trip with one message in flight, and every wait spins.
- Run: five invocations of the fourteen, ten runs each, at every placement the host declares:
  `smt`, CPUs 3 and 7, `ccx`, CPUs 3 and 2, two cores on the one L3, and unpinned. A one-thread
  bench has no `ccx` of its own.
- One binary, `e348cbb74d9f7c64`, built with rustc 1.99.0 from the tree one edit past `f27228d`,
  the version-of-record and `TODO.md` alone differing.
- Records: [records/mpsc-v3-fwlaptop.jsonl](../records/mpsc-v3-fwlaptop.jsonl), 1750 runs, every
  segment-switch count in them zero.
- Numbers are `analyze --compare`'s: each side's trimmed mean in ns, the difference as a percent
  of the first side's, and the claim, the smallest difference the pairing could call real.

## v3 against v2

`zcr-mpsc-v2` against `zcr-mpsc-v3`, `Multi` over two segments with `NoWake`, v2's geometry.

| bench | placement | v2 | v3 | d% | claim% | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `1t` | smt | 22.41 | 22.48 | +0.32 | 0.11 | detected |
| `1t` | unpinned | 22.40 | 22.48 | +0.36 | 0.08 | detected |
| `2t` | smt | 117.85 | 112.30 | -4.71 | 0.49 | detected |
| `2t` | ccx | 478.10 | 465.00 | -2.74 | 1.17 | detected |
| `2t` | unpinned | 486.91 | 471.71 | -3.12 | 2.42 | detected |

- At one thread v3 is 0.07 ns slower, a third of a percent.
- At two threads v3 is faster at every placement, by 3 to 5%.

## Multi over one segment against two

`zcr-mpsc-v3` against `zcr-mpsc-v3-*-1seg`, both `Multi` with `NoWake`.

| bench | placement | two | one | d% | claim% | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `1t` | smt | 22.48 | 22.47 | -0.02 | 0.06 | not seen |
| `1t` | unpinned | 22.48 | 22.48 | 0.00 | 0.03 | not seen |
| `2t` | smt | 112.30 | 112.31 | +0.01 | 0.40 | not seen |
| `2t` | ccx | 465.00 | 463.69 | -0.28 | 1.39 | not seen |
| `2t` | unpinned | 471.71 | 467.87 | -0.81 | 1.16 | not seen |

- A second segment costs nothing seen while no switch happens.

## Single against Multi over one segment

`-1seg` against `-single`, the geometry equal and the mode alone differing, under each wake.

| bench | wake | placement | `Multi` | `Single` | d% | claim% | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `1t` | `NoWake` | smt | 22.47 | 20.49 | -8.81 | 0.06 | detected |
| `1t` | `NoWake` | unpinned | 22.48 | 20.50 | -8.83 | 0.05 | detected |
| `1t` | `Futex` | smt | 23.31 | 21.11 | -9.45 | 0.06 | detected |
| `1t` | `Futex` | unpinned | 23.31 | 21.11 | -9.45 | 0.05 | detected |
| `2t` | `NoWake` | smt | 112.31 | 114.14 | +1.64 | 0.20 | detected |
| `2t` | `NoWake` | ccx | 463.69 | 459.80 | -0.84 | 1.00 | not seen |
| `2t` | `NoWake` | unpinned | 467.87 | 462.11 | -1.23 | 1.84 | not seen |
| `2t` | `Futex` | smt | 118.30 | 115.66 | -2.23 | 0.94 | detected |
| `2t` | `Futex` | ccx | 474.02 | 472.26 | -0.37 | 0.99 | not seen |
| `2t` | `Futex` | unpinned | 479.69 | 478.66 | -0.22 | 1.11 | not seen |

- At one thread `Single` is 2.0 to 2.2 ns faster, 9%, under both wakes and at both placements,
  and two earlier sessions of earlier binaries read the same, -8.62% and -8.67%.
- At two threads no difference holds: `not seen` four times of six, and the two `detected` at
  `smt` have opposite signs.

## Futex against NoWake

Each `NoWake` bench against its `-futex` twin. Nobody sleeps, so the difference is the wake checks
left on the message path, the producer's look at the waiting flag after its commit and the
consumer's fence at each half segment of releases, and not the cost of a sleep and a wake.

| bench | placement | `NoWake` | `Futex` | d% | claim% | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `1t` | smt | 22.48 | 23.31 | +3.69 | 0.09 | detected |
| `1t` | unpinned | 22.48 | 23.31 | +3.70 | 0.06 | detected |
| `1t-1seg` | smt | 22.47 | 23.31 | +3.72 | 0.08 | detected |
| `1t-1seg` | unpinned | 22.48 | 23.31 | +3.70 | 0.08 | detected |
| `1t-single` | smt | 20.49 | 21.11 | +2.99 | 0.03 | detected |
| `1t-single` | unpinned | 20.50 | 21.11 | +3.00 | 0.03 | detected |
| `2t` | smt | 112.30 | 118.66 | +5.67 | 0.32 | detected |
| `2t` | ccx | 465.00 | 478.97 | +3.00 | 0.96 | detected |
| `2t` | unpinned | 471.71 | 485.27 | +2.87 | 1.43 | detected |
| `2t-1seg` | smt | 112.31 | 118.30 | +5.34 | 0.80 | detected |
| `2t-1seg` | ccx | 463.69 | 474.02 | +2.23 | 1.00 | detected |
| `2t-1seg` | unpinned | 467.87 | 479.69 | +2.53 | 1.51 | detected |
| `2t-single` | smt | 114.14 | 115.66 | +1.33 | 0.84 | detected |
| `2t-single` | ccx | 459.80 | 472.26 | +2.71 | 0.90 | detected |
| `2t-single` | unpinned | 462.11 | 478.66 | +3.58 | 2.23 | detected |

- `Futex` is the slower in all fifteen: 0.6 to 0.8 ns at one thread, 3 to 4%, and 1.5 to 6.4 ns
  at `smt`, 10 to 14 ns at `ccx`, and 12 to 17 ns unpinned at two threads, 1 to 6%.

## What the numbers can carry

- One build of each bench: a mode or a wake is different code at different addresses, and with
  this repo's build settings layout alone moved single benches up to 8% ([build.md](build.md)).
  A difference in one bench at one placement is therefore not yet the parameter's.
- What repeats is: the `Futex` cost has one sign across fifteen rows of six benches, and the
  one-thread `Single` gain has one size across four rows and three sessions' binaries. We think
  both are the parameters' and not layout's.
- One host, and a laptop: its claims at two threads are 0.2 to 2.4%, where a measuring host's
  are tighter, and a ring's ranking has differed between hosts before
  ([Results by placement](../docs/report-guide.md#results-by-placement)).

## Whether the mode and the wake earn their place

Provisional, on the above, and zc-ring-x1's to decide.

- The mode: `Single` buys 2 ns of a 22 ns same-thread round trip and nothing shown where two
  threads hand off, which is what a ring between threads does, and `Multi` over one segment reads
  as `Multi` over two. We think the mode does not earn its place, and a ring that is always
  `Multi` loses only the same-thread case.
- The wake: a ring that can sleep pays 3 to 4% of every round trip when nobody sleeps, at every
  placement. We think that is too much to charge a ring that only spins, so the wake earns its
  place as a parameter unless its checks get cheaper, and what a sleep and a wake cost against a
  spin is not measured here.
EOF

The laptop session finished and the docs rung is in the working copy; full validation passes.

**What the session found** (one binary, v2's pair and the twelve v3 benches, five invocations at `smt`, `ccx` and unpinned, clock pinned at 2400 MHz, all 1750 runs with zero switches):

| question | one thread | two threads |
|---|---|---|
| v3 against v2 | v3 0.3% slower (0.07 ns) | v3 3 to 5% faster at every placement |
| `Multi` over one segment against two | not seen | not seen |
| `Single` against `Multi` over one segment | `Single` 9% faster (2.0 to 2.2 ns), under both wakes | no consistent difference: 4 of 6 not seen, the other two opposite in sign |
| `Futex` against `NoWake`, nobody sleeping | `Futex` 3 to 4% slower (0.6 to 0.8 ns) | `Futex` 1 to 6% slower at every placement |

- **The wake**: `Futex` is slower in all fifteen rows. I think that cost is real and too much to charge a ring that only spins, so the wake earns its place as a parameter unless its checks get cheaper.
- **The mode**: `Single` only helps when one thread does both ends, which is not what a ring between threads does. I think the mode does not earn its place.
- **How far to trust it**: one laptop and one build of each bench. Layout alone has moved single benches up to 8% in this repo, so only the results that repeat across rows carry weight, and the note says it is provisional until the measuring hosts repeat it.

The plain version: the new ring is a little faster than the old one between threads. The one-segment-only mode buys nothing in real use, so it could go. The ability to sleep costs a few percent even when unused, so it is worth keeping optional.

**What is in the working copy**
- `notes/mpsc-v3-mode-wake.md`: the four tables, the caveats, and the provisional answer.
- `records/mpsc-v3-fwlaptop.jsonl`: the session, 8.3 MiB.

- `notes/README.md`: a pointer to the note.

- **jj setting**: jj refuses new files over 1 MiB, so I raised `snapshot.max-new-file-size` to 10 MB for this clone only (a repo-local setting, not committed).
- **Dirty binary**: the session's records are stamped `dirty`, because the binary was built after this rung's version bump and before its commit. Only the version-of-record and `TODO.md` differed from the futex rung's commit.
- **Todo rank**: I put the follow-up entry first in `## Todo`; move it if it should rank lower. I folded the laptop's `pin_freq` failure into that entry as a bullet rather than filing a bug.

The twelve mpsc v3 benches vary the ring's two type parameters, its
segment mode and its wake, but what they measured is in records and
nowhere a reader finds it, so the question they were built for, do
the mode and the wake earn their place, has no written answer.

* The comparisons have no home.
  - A note holds them as four tables: v3 against v2, `Multi` over
    one segment against two, `Single` against `Multi` over one
    segment, and `Futex` against `NoWake`, each at every placement
    the host declares.

    build of each bench, and gives its answer as provisional.
* The tables rest on a session nobody else can read back.
  - The session's records are kept beside the other sessions', so
    `analyze` reproduces every row.
* The session ran on a laptop, the measuring hosts being out of
  reach.
  - A Todo entry repeats it on the measuring hosts, revises the note
    from them, and only then tells zc-ring-x1.
```

229	## Close-out shapes
230	
231	The two shapes a ladder can land in, chosen by the user and recorded at close-out, executed at
232	[Land](#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land) ([Close-out](../AGENTS.md#close-out)). A single-step cycle
233	is one commit and lands as it is:
234	
235	- **trapezoid**, the current default: a merge commit whose first parent is the trunk and whose
236	  second is the ladder, so `git log --first-parent` reads one commit per cycle while every rung
237	  stays reachable. Reshaped at Land by the [recipe below](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe) and published
238	  by the landing fast-forward itself.
239	- **keep separate**, one commit per rung on `main`, when the decomposition itself is informative.
240	
241	Squash is not a shape: each rung's `ochid:` trailer is a change id, a squash keeps one and drops the
242	rest, and every agent-repo commit that pointed at a dropped rung is left dangling ([Cycle
243	shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)).
244	
245	**Preview before choosing.** The cycle's net change is the tree diff from `<base>` to the tip,
246	whatever shape the commits between are in: `jj diff --from <base> --to <tip>`, or the gitk range
247	described in [Read a change in gitk at full context](#read-a-change-in-gitk-at-full-context). The
248	trapezoid keeps each rung reachable while `git log --first-parent` shows this net diff once landed,
249	and keep separate shows the rungs themselves. The choice is made on what `main` will carry.
250	
251	## Read a change in gitk at full context
252	
253	gitk renders a change three ways, and at full context each answers a different question. Raise
254	"Lines of context" to the longest file's length, or to a large number such as 1000 (`--context 1000`
255	is the CLI equivalent), to see the entire file, then select:
256	
257	- **New version**: the file as it now is, with the added lines lit. This is what the permanent
258	  branch will carry, so it is the view for judging whether a change reads as one thing.
259	- **Old version**: the file as it was, with the removed lines lit. It answers what the change costs,
260	  which a diff states only as minus lines out of context.
261	- **Diff**: the two interleaved. At full context it is the whole file with the edit marked in place,
262	  which is the reading a reviewer wants when the edit is small and the file is not.
263	
264	The above reads one commit at a time and is useful. Another mode is to see how several commits
265	together changed the tree since a given `<base>` commit. To do that:
266	
267	- Hover over the commit you want as the `<base>`, right click and select "Mark this commit".
268	- Hover over any commit above the `<base>`, right click and select "Diff marked commit -> this".
269	
270	Now New version, Old version and Diff show the net change of everything between `<base>` and `this`.
271	If `<base>` is the parent of the `opening` commit and `this` is the `closing`, that is the cycle's
272	net change, and it can help you decide what shape to choose ([Close-out shapes](#close-out-shapes)).
273	
274	## Trapezoid close-out recipe
275	
276	The reshape behind the trapezoid shape, run at [Land](#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land) step 2: the
277	close-out commit, pushed linearly by the closing rung, becomes a merge whose first parent is the
278	trunk line and whose second parent is the cycle's ladder. Nothing here publishes, the merge goes out
279	with Land's fast-forward.
280	
281	```
282	  main line   ...--<base>------------------<closeout>--
283	                      \                    /
284	  ladder             <rung-1>--...--<tip>-+
285	```
286	
287	- `<base>`: the **parent of the ladder's first rung**, the trunk position when the cycle opened. It
288	  becomes the first parent. Not always the previous close-out: a cycle landed linearly since
289	  (keep-separate shape, or a single-step cycle) sits on the trunk line and must stay there.
290	- `<tip>`: the cycle's last commit before the close-out. It becomes the second parent.
291	- `<closeout>`: the close-out commit, reshaped here.
292	
293	1. `jj rebase -r <closeout> --onto <base> --onto <tip>`: `<closeout>` becomes the merge. Parent
294	   order is the argument order.
295	2. `jj new <closeout>`: an empty `@` above the merge. The bookmark followed the rewrite on its own.
296	   What step 1 leaves misplaced is the working copy: `jj rebase -r` re-parents descendants onto the
297	   rebased commit's old parent, so the empty `@` lands beside the merge on `<tip>` and the tree
298	   reverts to pre-close-out content, which looks alarming and is not.
299	3. Verify two parents: `jj log -r <closeout> -T 'parents.map(|p| p.change_id().short(8))'` must list
300	   both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>` is an ancestor of `<tip>` (observed at
301	   three consecutive close-outs), but a collapsed merge is indistinguishable from a correct one in
302	   `jj log --no-graph`.
303	
304	Details:
305	
306	- **Trailers survive.** The restore's squash and the reshape change `<closeout>`'s SHA but not its
307	  change id, so the `ochid:` trailers stamped at the closing push stay valid in both directions.
308	- **Immutability.** No flag is needed: a topic bookmark's commits are not on `trunk()` until Land's
309	  fast-forward.
310	
311	Recovery:
312	
313	- **Nothing is published until Land's fast-forward**, so the whole reshape is undoable with
314	  `jj undo` / `jj op restore`.
315	- **A collapsed or mis-parented merge**: undo and redo step 1 with the corrected revisions. Do not
316	  land a shape you did not intend. After the fast-forward the remote boundary is crossed and
317	  recovery is forward-only.
318	- **Working copy left beside the merge** (step 2 skipped): `jj new <closeout>` after the fact. Any
319	  commit made in the meantime branches off `<tip>` and needs a rebase onto the merge.

## Close-out shapes

The two shapes a ladder can land in, chosen by the user and recorded at close-out, executed at
[Land](#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land) ([Close-out](../AGENTS.md#close-out)). A single-step cycle
is one commit and lands as it is:

- **trapezoid**, the current default: a merge commit whose first parent is the trunk and whose
  second is the ladder, so `git log --first-parent` reads one commit per cycle while every rung
  stays reachable. Reshaped at Land by the [recipe below](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe) and published
  by the landing fast-forward itself.
- **keep separate**, one commit per rung on `main`, when the decomposition itself is informative.

Squash is not a shape: each rung's `ochid:` trailer is a change id, a squash keeps one and drops the
rest, and every agent-repo commit that pointed at a dropped rung is left dangling ([Cycle
shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)).

**Preview before choosing.** The cycle's net change is the tree diff from `<base>` to the tip,
whatever shape the commits between are in: `jj diff --from <base> --to <tip>`, or the gitk range
described in [Read a change in gitk at full context](#read-a-change-in-gitk-at-full-context). The
trapezoid keeps each rung reachable while `git log --first-parent` shows this net diff once landed,
and keep separate shows the rungs themselves. The choice is made on what `main` will carry.

## Read a change in gitk at full context

gitk renders a change three ways, and at full context each answers a different question. Raise
"Lines of context" to the longest file's length, or to a large number such as 1000 (`--context 1000`
is the CLI equivalent), to see the entire file, then select:

- **New version**: the file as it now is, with the added lines lit. This is what the permanent
  branch will carry, so it is the view for judging whether a change reads as one thing.
- **Old version**: the file as it was, with the removed lines lit. It answers what the change costs,
  which a diff states only as minus lines out of context.
- **Diff**: the two interleaved. At full context it is the whole file with the edit marked in place,
  which is the reading a reviewer wants when the edit is small and the file is not.

The above reads one commit at a time and is useful. Another mode is to see how several commits
together changed the tree since a given `<base>` commit. To do that:

- Hover over the commit you want as the `<base>`, right click and select "Mark this commit".
- Hover over any commit above the `<base>`, right click and select "Diff marked commit -> this".

Now New version, Old version and Diff show the net change of everything between `<base>` and `this`.
If `<base>` is the parent of the `opening` commit and `this` is the `closing`, that is the cycle's
net change, and it can help you decide what shape to choose ([Close-out shapes](#close-out-shapes)).

## Trapezoid close-out recipe

The reshape behind the trapezoid shape, run at [Land](#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land) step 2: the
close-out commit, pushed linearly by the closing rung, becomes a merge whose first parent is the
trunk line and whose second parent is the cycle's ladder. Nothing here publishes, the merge goes out
with Land's fast-forward.

```
  main line   ...--<base>------------------<closeout>--
                      \                    /
  ladder             <rung-1>--...--<tip>-+
```

- `<base>`: the **parent of the ladder's first rung**, the trunk position when the cycle opened. It
  becomes the first parent. Not always the previous close-out: a cycle landed linearly since
  (keep-separate shape, or a single-step cycle) sits on the trunk line and must stay there.
- `<tip>`: the cycle's last commit before the close-out. It becomes the second parent.
- `<closeout>`: the close-out commit, reshaped here.

1. `jj rebase -r <closeout> --onto <base> --onto <tip>`: `<closeout>` becomes the merge. Parent
   order is the argument order.
2. `jj new <closeout>`: an empty `@` above the merge. The bookmark followed the rewrite on its own.

3. Verify two parents: `jj log -r <closeout> -T 'parents.map(|p| p.change_id().short(8))'` must list
   both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>` is an ancestor of `<tip>` (observed at

Details:

- **Trailers survive.** The restore's squash and the reshape change `<closeout>`'s SHA but not its
  change id, so the `ochid:` trailers stamped at the closing push stay valid in both directions.
- **Immutability.** No flag is needed: a topic bookmark's commits are not on `trunk()` until Land's
